prop:hecke-1d-irrep-closed-form-characte:
Proposition Universal closed form for 1-d Hecke irrep characters: \chi^{(n)}_q(\beta) = q^w \cdot ([2]_q/2)^m and \chi^{(1^n)}_q(\beta) = (-q^{-1})^w \cdot (-[2]_q/2)^m for typed braids of any n. Conditional on Quarks as Borromean-linked unknots in the exceptional divisor.

Let n \geq 2. Let \beta \in B_n be a typed braid encoded as a sequence of crossings in \{\sigma_i,\, \sigma_i^{-1},\, \sigma_i - h/2\cdot\mathbf{1}\}, with h = q - q^{-1}. The q-character on each 1-dimensional irreducible representation of H_n(q) obeys the universal closed form:

\boxed{
  \chi^{(n)}_q(\beta) \;=\; q^{w(\beta)} \cdot \bigl(\tfrac{[2]_q}{2}\bigr)^{m(\beta)}
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  \chi^{(1^n)}_q(\beta) \;=\; \bigl(-q^{-1}\bigr)^{w(\beta)} \cdot \bigl(-\tfrac{[2]_q}{2}\bigr)^{m(\beta)},
}

where:

  • w(\beta) = \#(\sigma_i) - \#(\sigma_i^{-1}) is the writhe.
  • m(\beta) is the number of averaged (operator-valued \sigma_i - h/2) crossings.
  • [2]_q = q + q^{-1} is the quantum integer.

This form is independent of n. The choice of 1-d irrep (V_{(n)} trivial or V_{(1^n)} sign) dictates the eigenvalue \lambda_\sigma \in \{+q,\, -q^{-1}\}.

The identity is algebraic and sits on the aether side of the wall. It holds over any commutative coefficient ring in which q is a unit and 2 is invertible; the minimal such ring is \mathbb{Z}[\tfrac12][q, q^{-1}], the factor \tfrac12 being required only by the averaged crossing \sigma_i - h/2. Evaluation at the aether parameter q_0 is a downstream specialization and is not used in the derivation.
prf:hecke-1d-irrep-closed-form-character:
Proof Proof of hecke 1d irrep closed form character. A 1-dimensional irrep V_\lambda of H_n(q) is determined by the generator-image scalar \rho_\lambda(\sigma_i) = \lambda_\sigma, which by the Iwahori-Hecke relation (\sigma_i - q)(\sigma_i + q^{-1}) = 0 must satisfy \lambda_\sigma \in \{+q,\, -q^{-1}\}. The two choices give the trivial and sign 1-d irreps respectively (per the Hecke branching trace decomposition).

For a typed braid \beta = c_1 c_2 \cdots c_L with crossings c_\ell \in \{\sigma_i,\, \sigma_i^{-1},\, \sigma_i - h/2\}, the 1-d action is multiplicative:

  \rho_\lambda(\beta) \;=\; \prod_{\ell=1}^{L} \rho_\lambda(c_\ell),

with the three crossing types contributing:

\begin{aligned}
  \rho_\lambda(\sigma_i)              &= \lambda_\sigma, \\
  \rho_\lambda(\sigma_i^{-1})         &= \lambda_\sigma^{-1}, \\
  \rho_\lambda(\sigma_i - \tfrac{h}{2}\mathbf{1})
                                       &= \lambda_\sigma - \tfrac{h}{2}.
\end{aligned}

Hence

  \rho_\lambda(\beta)
   \;=\;
   \lambda_\sigma^{w(\beta)} \cdot
   \bigl(\lambda_\sigma - \tfrac{h}{2}\bigr)^{m(\beta)} .

The q-character \chi^\lambda_q(\beta) = \mathrm{tr}_{V_\lambda} \rho_\lambda(\beta) = \rho_\lambda(\beta) (trace on 1-d space). Substituting \lambda_\sigma = +q and using q - h/2 = q - (q - q^{-1})/2 = (q + q^{-1})/2 = [2]_q/2:

  \chi^{(n)}_q(\beta) \;=\; q^{w(\beta)} \cdot \bigl(\tfrac{[2]_q}{2}\bigr)^{m(\beta)}.

Similarly \lambda_\sigma = -q^{-1} gives -q^{-1} - h/2 = -[2]_q/2, so

  \chi^{(1^n)}_q(\beta) \;=\; (-q^{-1})^{w(\beta)} \cdot \bigl(-\tfrac{[2]_q}{2}\bigr)^{m(\beta)}.

The formulas hold for every n because the 1-d Hecke irreps' generator eigenvalues \pm q^{\pm 1} are aether-derived — they come from the Hecke quadratic relation, not from any n-specific representation combinatorics. \blacksquare

Verification

Bit-exact at 50 dps for all atoms in \{p, n, D, T, {}^{3}\mathrm{He}\} (n \in \{3, 5, 8\}).

Role in the τ_M decomposition

The full Markov trace at any n decomposes as

  \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta)
   \;=\;
   y_{(n)} \cdot \chi^{(n)}_q(\beta)
   \;+\;
   \sum_{\substack{\lambda \vdash n \\ \dim V_\lambda \geq 2}}
     y_\lambda \cdot \chi^\lambda_q(\beta)
   \;+\;
   y_{(1^n)} \cdot \chi^{(1^n)}_q(\beta),

where the 1-d backbone (y_{(n)} \chi^{(n)} + y_{(1^n)} \chi^{(1^n)}) is fully closed-form aether-derivable for any n via the formulas above, and the \dim \geq 2 middle terms require the Hoefsmit seminormal matrix characters (per the Hecke branching trace decomposition).

Recursion to higher n

For n \geq 4 the trivial and sign irreps remain 1-dimensional with the same generator eigenvalues, so this closed form extends without modification to {}^{4}He (H_{12}), {}^{6}Li (H_{18}), and all heavier isotopes. Higher-dimensional irreps grow combinatorially (per Robinson-Schensted), but their contribution to the 1-d backbone of \mathrm{tr}_M is captured by exactly the same closed forms — only the y_\lambda weights and the Hoefsmit matrices of the \dim \geq 2 blocks change with n.

The entire 1-d slice of the Wedderburn decomposition of \mathrm{tr}_M is therefore a finite closed-form expression in (q, w, m), with no n-dependence in the formula beyond the choice of trivial-vs-sign irrep.

prop:phi-b-bar-parity-decomposition:
Proposition Bar-parity (sinh/cosh) decomposition under the bar involution.

Bar-parity (sinh/cosh) decomposition under the bar involution

Let R be a commutative ring and \sigma\colon R\to R a ring involution — the bar q\mapsto q^{-1}. For every f\in R,

2f \;=\; \underbrace{(f+\sigma f)}_{\text{bar-even}} \;+\; \underbrace{(f-\sigma f)}_{\text{bar-odd}},
\qquad
\sigma(f+\sigma f)=f+\sigma f,\qquad \sigma(f-\sigma f)=-(f-\sigma f).

The bar-even part is fixed by \sigma; the bar-odd part is negated. The decomposition is unique and holds over any commutative ring.

Unitary phases are bar-odd: the fibre-saddle rigidity

Let R be a commutative ring with a ring involution \sigma, and call u \in R \sigma-unitary when

  \sigma(u)\,u = 1

(the ring-involution form of |u| = 1). Then:

  1. 1 is \sigma-unitary, and \sigma-unitaries are closed under multiplication;
  2. (rigidity) a bar-even \sigma-unitary is an involution: \sigma(u) = u and \sigma(u)\,u = 1 imply u^2 = 1;
  3. equivalently, a \sigma-unitary with u^2 \neq 1 satisfies \sigma(u) \neq u — every genuine phase carries a nontrivial bar-odd part.

On the fibre saddle — real b, so q = e^{2\pi i b^2} is a root of unity — the Faddeev quantum dilogarithm is unimodular: |\Phi_b(z)| = 1 for real z (witnessed on the validated evaluator at the \zeta_4, \zeta_5^2, \zeta_6 and self-dual points; analytically this is the reflection w \mapsto -\bar w of the Faddeev contour integral). So the fibre-saddle \Phi_b is a \sigma-unitary in the sense above, with \sigma the bar involution (archimedean instance: complex conjugation).

The rigidity clause then forces the structure of the ladder factorisation F(q) = F_{\text{even}}(q)\cdot F_{\text{odd}}(q): a phase beyond \pm 1 cannot sit on the bar-even face. The unimodular fibre-saddle \Phi_b is therefore intrinsically a bar-odd carrier, and the phase reframe \mathfrak{Q}_\beta/Q_A = \cos\Phi(u) is the natural bar-odd form for the decay channel. prf:q-bessel-c-k-recurrence-cfinite:
Proof Throughout, q and the order \nu are formal parameters in a field; no archimedean structure is used. Write (x;q)_k = \prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\bigl(1 - x q^{j}\bigr) for the q-Pochhammer symbol, with (x;q)_0 = 1.

Step 1 — the closed-form coefficients and their ratio. The Hahn–Exton q-Bessel function of order \nu has power-series coefficients

c_k \;=\; \frac{(-1)^k\, q^{k(k-1)/2}}{(q;q)_k\,\bigl(q^{\nu+1};q\bigr)_k}, \qquad k \ge 0 .

Compare consecutive coefficients. The sign contributes a factor -1; the Gaussian exponent contributes q^{k(k+1)/2 - k(k-1)/2} = q^{k}; and each q-Pochhammer symbol gains exactly one factor,

\frac{(q;q)_{k+1}}{(q;q)_k} = 1 - q^{k+1},
\qquad
\frac{\bigl(q^{\nu+1};q\bigr)_{k+1}}{\bigl(q^{\nu+1};q\bigr)_k} = 1 - q^{\nu+k+1}.

Multiplying out, the coefficients satisfy the first-order q-recurrence

c_{k+1}\,\bigl(1 - q^{k+1}\bigr)\bigl(1 - q^{\nu+k+1}\bigr) \;=\; -\,q^{k}\, c_k
\qquad (\star)

for all k \ge 0.

Step 2 — first-order recurrences integrate to a product. Conversely, (\star) determines the sequence from its seed. Let (r_k)_{k \ge 0} be any sequence of scalars and suppose a sequence (c_k) satisfies c_{k+1} = r_k\, c_k for all k. Then, by induction on k,

c_k \;=\; c_0 \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} r_j ,

the empty product being 1 at k = 0 and the induction step reading c_{k+1} = r_k\, c_k = c_0 \prod_{j=0}^{k} r_j. For generic parameters the denominators \bigl(1 - q^{k+1}\bigr)\bigl(1 - q^{\nu+k+1}\bigr) never vanish (vanishing requires q a root of unity or q^{\nu+1} \in q^{-\mathbb{N}}), so (\star) is of this form with ratio

r_k \;=\; \frac{-\,q^{k}}{\bigl(1 - q^{k+1}\bigr)\bigl(1 - q^{\nu+k+1}\bigr)} ,

and every solution of (\star) is the q-hypergeometric product c_k = c_0 \prod_{j=0}^{k-1} r_j. In particular the closed form of Step 1 is the unique solution with c_0 = 1.

Step 3 — q-holonomic, with C-finite as the degeneration. The ratio r_k depends on k through q^{k}: the recurrence (\star) is first-order linear with q^{k}-dependent coefficients, so the sequence (c_k) is q-holonomic. A constant-coefficient (C-finite) recurrence arises exactly in the degenerate case of a k-independent ratio: if c_{k+1} = \rho\, c_k for a single scalar \rho, the product of Step 2 collapses to the geometric sequence

c_k = c_0\, \rho^{k},

which is C-finite of order 1 with characteristic root \rho. This degeneration occurs in the rational limit of the underlying q-difference kernel (in particular after the q \to 1 contraction, where the rescaled ratio (1-q)^2\, c_{k+1}/c_k tends to -1/\bigl((k+1)(\nu+k+1)\bigr), the coefficient ratio of the classical Bessel series), never for the genuine q-Bessel ratio r_k.

Step 4 — consequence for the precision-ladder coefficients. At the fibre level the ladder kernel is a q-Bessel object, not a rational function; by Step 3 its coefficient sequence therefore admits no low-order constant-coefficient recurrence, while the dominant-root structure of the associated q-difference kernel survives. The canonical ladder values c_2, \ldots, c_{10}, expanded in the ladder variable u \approx 0.00852, exhibit exactly this pair of signatures: no constant-coefficient recurrence of order at most 4 fits them, while the tail ratio approaches the reciprocal pole location, c_{k+1}/c_k \to 1/u \approx 117.4. \blacksquare

This argument supplies the fibre-level skeleton of the recursion only: the identification of the ladder with a q-Bessel coefficient sequence is a formal statement in q and \nu, and the production c_k ladder remains calibration-anchored.
prf:q-bessel-second-order-qdifference:
Proof Throughout, q and the order \nu are formal parameters in a field; the argument is purely q-difference-algebraic. Write (x;q)_k = \prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\bigl(1 - x q^{j}\bigr) for the q-Pochhammer symbol, and let

g(w) \;=\; \sum_{k \ge 0} c_k\, w^{k},
\qquad
c_k \;=\; \frac{(-1)^k\, q^{k(k-1)/2}}{(q;q)_k\,\bigl(q^{\nu+1};q\bigr)_k},

be the generating function of the Hahn–Exton q-Bessel coefficients of order \nu. By the contiguity recurrence, the coefficients satisfy the first-order relation

c_k\,\bigl(1 - q^{k}\bigr)\bigl(1 - q^{\nu+k}\bigr) \;=\; -\,q^{k-1}\, c_{k-1},
\qquad k \ge 1. \qquad (\star)

Step 1 — assemble the three q-shifts. The q-shifted series are g(qw) = \sum_{k} c_k\, q^{k} w^{k} and g(q^2 w) = \sum_{k} c_k\, q^{2k} w^{k}. Hence

q^{\nu}\, g(q^2 w) - \bigl(1 + q^{\nu}\bigr)\, g(q w) + g(w)
\;=\; \sum_{k \ge 0} c_k \Bigl( q^{\nu+2k} - \bigl(1 + q^{\nu}\bigr) q^{k} + 1 \Bigr) w^{k},

and the bracket factors,

q^{\nu+2k} - \bigl(1 + q^{\nu}\bigr) q^{k} + 1
\;=\; \bigl(1 - q^{k}\bigr)\bigl(1 - q^{\nu+k}\bigr),

as one checks by expanding the right-hand side. This factorisation into the (\star) denominator is the reason the second-order operator collapses onto the first-order recurrence.

Step 2 — the source term. Re-indexing a single q-shift multiplied by w,

w\, g(q w) \;=\; \sum_{k \ge 0} c_k\, q^{k} w^{k+1} \;=\; \sum_{k \ge 1} c_{k-1}\, q^{k-1} w^{k}.

Step 3 — coefficient comparison. Combining Steps 1 and 2, the w^{k} coefficient of

q^{\nu}\, g(q^2 w) - \bigl(1 + q^{\nu} - w\bigr)\, g(q w) + g(w)

is c_0 \bigl(1 - q^{0}\bigr)\bigl(1 - q^{\nu}\bigr) = 0 for k = 0, and

c_k\,\bigl(1 - q^{k}\bigr)\bigl(1 - q^{\nu+k}\bigr) + q^{k-1}\, c_{k-1}

for k \ge 1. By (\star) every coefficient vanishes, so the generating function satisfies the second-order q-difference equation

q^{\nu}\, g(q^2 w) \;-\; \bigl(1 + q^{\nu} - w\bigr)\, g(q w) \;+\; g(w) \;=\; 0.
\qquad (\star\star)

Writing \eta for the q-shift operator (\eta f)(w) = f(qw), equation (\star\star) reads \bigl[\,q^{\nu}\eta^{2} - \bigl(1 + q^{\nu} - w\bigr)\eta + 1\,\bigr] g = 0: a genuine second-order (three-point: w, qw, q^2 w) q-difference operator, whose linear term +w in the middle coefficient is the source making the coefficient ladder descend.

Step 4 — equivalence of (\star\star) and (\star). The computation in Steps 1–3 is reversible: (\star\star) holds if and only if every w^{k} coefficient vanishes, and for k \ge 1 that vanishing is exactly (\star). The "second order" refers to the q-difference order (three q-shifted arguments); on the coefficients the equation collapses to a two-term relation between consecutive c_k, precisely because the middle coefficient factors through the (\star) denominator as in Step 1. Equivalently, shifting the index to k+1, the coefficient relation is

\Bigl( q^{\nu+2k+2} - q^{k+1} - q^{\nu+k+1} + 1 \Bigr) c_{k+1} + q^{k}\, c_k = 0,
\qquad
q^{\nu+2k+2} - q^{k+1} - q^{\nu+k+1} + 1 = \bigl(1 - q^{k+1}\bigr)\bigl(1 - q^{\nu+k+1}\bigr).

Step 5 — classical contraction. In the limit q \to 1^{-} the rescaled operator contracts to the ordinary Bessel operator w\, g'' + (\nu + 1)\, g' + g acting on g(w): the denominators degenerate as 1 - q^{k} \sim k\,(1-q) and 1 - q^{\nu+k} \sim (\nu+k)(1-q), so the rescaled coefficient ratio satisfies \lim_{q \to 1^{-}} (1-q)^{2}\, c_k / c_{k-1} = -1/\bigl(k(\nu+k)\bigr), the coefficient recurrence of the classical Bessel series \sum_{k} (-1)^k z^k / \bigl(k!\, (\nu+1)_k\bigr) in a formal variable z, where (\nu+1)_k is the ordinary Pochhammer symbol. \blacksquare

This is a fibre-level structural result: q and \nu are formal parameters, and no aether evaluation is involved.

prop:faddeev-phib-uniqueness:
Proposition Uniqueness of the modular-double \Phi_b: strip growth pins the quantum dilogarithm up to scale. Conditional on the Faddeev shift-class and its strip-growth characterization. Fix the aether parameter b = b(t) on the product-supported branch \mathrm{Im} b^2 > 0 (in particular the physical map b(t) = \sqrt{t/2\pi}\,e^{i\pi/4} with t = \ln q_0 > 0). Let \Phi_1 be any solution of the two modular-double q-difference equations of the non-compact quantum dilogarithm at b that is (i) comparable in modulus to the canonical product \Phi_b — some C > 0 bounds each of \lVert\Phi_1\rVert,\ \lVert\Phi_b\rVert by C times the other — and (ii) meromorphic on \mathbb{C} and continuous wherever \Phi_b \neq 0. Then \Phi_1 = c\,\Phi_b for a single constant c, on the nonvanishing locus of \Phi_b.

Here \Phi_b is the modular-double product

\Phi_b(z) \;=\;
\frac{\prod_{k\ge 0}\bigl(1 + e^{i\pi b^2(2k+1)}\,e^{2\pi b z}\bigr)}
     {\prod_{k\ge 0}\bigl(1 + e^{-i\pi b^{-2}(2k+1)}\,e^{2\pi z/b}\bigr)},

which on the branch \mathrm{Im} b^2 > 0 converges and equals the Faddeev contour integral. It is the canonical solution — it satisfies both hypotheses with c = 1, so the admissible class is nonempty and the constant is genuinely pinned.

Why the shift equations alone do not suffice

The two first-order q-difference equations are invariant under multiplication by any function elliptic for the aether lattice \langle ib, i/b\rangle: the shift multipliers cancel in the ratio \Phi_1/\Phi_b, which is therefore doubly periodic. A nonconstant elliptic factor — a full-lattice Weierstrass \wp — is thus compatible with the difference equations and would give a second, non-proportional solution. Rigidity requires two further inputs the shift class does not record, and one growth condition:

  1. The inversion relation \Phi_b(x)\Phi_b(-x) = c_0 excludes the even part of the elliptic freedom algebraically.
  2. \sigma-unitarity (self-duality, \lvert\Phi_b\rvert = 1) excludes the bar-even reciprocal-odd part algebraically.
  3. The residual non-\sigma-fixed reciprocal-odd freedom is excluded analytically: a nonconstant elliptic function has poles, so it violates the boundedness the strip-growth comparability enforces on the ratio.

Standing

Every analytic ingredient is established without contour integration. The product \Phi_b is meromorphic on the branch (its two infinite products are entire, as locally-uniform limits of entire partial products), its zeros are isolated (each factor's zeros form a discrete lattice, and the products vanish only where a factor does), and the strip growth follows from elementary product-norm bounds. The ratio's global boundedness is derived from comparability by a removable-singularity extension, and the two periodicity loci are dense because their complements are countable unions of the factor lattices. The remaining hypotheses — that the second solution is comparable, meromorphic, and continuous where finite — are the honest content of "the physical \Phi_b is a bona-fide meromorphic function", not a mathematical gap.

Published form of the product and the growth

Faddeev, Kashaev and Volkov write the non-compact quantum dilogarithm, for \mathrm{Re}\,b > 0, \mathrm{Im}\,b \ge 0, as a ratio of two q-exponentials, e_b(z) = (e^{2\pi(z + c_b)b}; q^2)_\infty \,/\, (e^{2\pi(z - c_b)b^{-1}}; \bar q^2)_\infty with q = e^{i\pi b^2} and \bar q = e^{-i\pi b^{-2}}, a meromorphic function on \mathbb{C} whose zeros and poles lie on the lattices \mp(c_b + mib + nib^{-1}), m, n \ge 0 [faddeev-kashaev-volkov2000, §6.2, eq. (21)]. They give its behaviour as |z| \to \infty in four sectors fixed by \arg z relative to \arg b: constant 1, a Gaussian e^{i\pi z^2} times a constant, and two regimes given by Jacobi theta functions [faddeev-kashaev-volkov2000, §6.2, eq. (22)]. This is the explicit form of the product displayed above and of the sector-wise growth that the strip-growth hypothesis (i) compares against; the uniqueness argument above is not taken from that paper.
